extracted.intended_audience: ICLR 2022 reviewers (assigned peer reviewers for ICLR conference submissions)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and procedural requirements for reviewing submitted papers for ICLR 2022: reading and evaluating submissions, writing structured reviews, participating in discussion, reporting ethics/conflicts, and providing final recommendations to area chairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timeliness and substantive reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Your reviews are timely and substantive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the timeline (write reviews by review deadline; provide final recommendation by final recommendation deadline). During the discussion phase be responsive (able to respond to comments/requests within 3 business days). Reviews should be both delivered on time and contain meaningful, detailed content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adhere to Code of Ethics and Code of Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers must adhere to ICLR's Code of Ethics (CoE) and Code of Conduct in their reviewer role.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check assigned papers for conflicts with the CoE and mark them in your CoE report. If uncertain about violations, reach out to your area chair. For other violations (plagiarism, double submission, formatting/length), contact the AC or PC via official OpenReview comment with appropriate readership restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create and maintain OpenReview profile (procedural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Create your OpenReview profile and link your DBLP profile (by stated deadline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep profile information up to date (co-authors, institutions) to help conflict-of-interest detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bidding on papers (procedural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Participate in the bidding process within the specified bidding window.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bid on papers during the bidding period to help the assignment process (specified dates). If you encounter a paper presenting a conflict of interest while bidding, choose 'Very Low' for that paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Main reviewer task: write a constructive, thorough review
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a review that determines whether the submission brings sufficient value and new knowledge to the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize reviews with a positive summary, comprehensive list of strengths and weaknesses, clear accept/reject recommendation with 1-2 key reasons, supporting arguments, questions for authors, and constructive suggestions to improve the paper.

rubrics_metrics.name: Engage in discussion and update recommendation
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss with authors, other reviewers, and ACs to clarify and improve the paper during the discussion phase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be actively engaged and responsive during the discussion phase; update your review and final recommendation taking into account new information and revisions. Maintain openness to changing your initial recommendation either more positive or more negative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flagging ethics and policy violations
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag any potential CoE violations and/or other concerns during review and discussion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indicate CoE violations when submitting the CoE report for that paper. For other policy violations (plagiarism, double submission, paper length, formatting), contact the AC or PC as appropriate by sending an official comment with appropriate readership restrictions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thorough reading and literature checking
rubrics_metrics.description: Carefully read the entire paper and look up related work and citations to comprehensively evaluate it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give yourself sufficient time to read. Be sure to check references and related literature to judge novelty and placement in the field; include references to back up claims about prior work where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the objective of the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the goal of the paper (e.g., address known application/problem, new application/problem, theoretical finding, or combination) and evaluate accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different objectives require different considerations for potential value and impact; tailor your assessment to the stated aim of the submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess clarity of presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether the submission is clear and understandable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Point out unclear explanations; include suggestions and requests for clarification. Be generous and summarize the paper's claims as a service to authors and readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess technical correctness
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine whether theoretical results and algorithmic claims are correct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check proofs, derivations, and algorithm descriptions for correctness and completeness; ask targeted questions if something seems wrong or incomplete.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess experimental rigor and reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether experiments are rigorous and reproducible and whether they support the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check for adequate baselines, hyperparameter settings, ablation studies, statistical significance where appropriate, and sufficient experimental detail for reproducibility. Suggest limited additional experiments only when justified to push the paper toward acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess novelty / contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge whether the submission presents novel findings (theoretical, algorithmic, empirical) or a meaningful contribution to the community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide concrete comparisons to prior work; indicate if novelty is incremental versus substantial and why. Use literature checks to support your view.

rubrics_metrics.name: Support of claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide whether the paper supports its claims through correct results and rigorous evidence (theoretical or empirical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Verify that claimed performance, theoretical guarantees, or conclusions are backed by the presented results and analyses. If not, request clarifications or appropriate additional validation with a justification for why these are necessary for acceptance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use 'not interesting' as a rejection criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: A paper should not be rejected solely because it is not personally interesting to a reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the broader ICLR community; research may have value to others now or in the future. Base decisions on objective criteria (novelty, correctness, rigor, contribution), not subjective interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of supplementary material
rubrics_metrics.description: Supplementary material is optional to read but can often answer questions arising from the main paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is not necessary to read supplementary material, but reviewers are encouraged to consult it before asking authors questions if it may resolve issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requests for additional experiments must be justified and limited
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers may ask for additional experiments but must justify why they are necessary to push the paper over the acceptance threshold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: New experiments should not significantly change the submission's content; they should be limited in scope and serve to validate existing results rather than introduce new directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expectations about state-of-the-art
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of state-of-the-art (SOTA) results is not by itself grounds for rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers can bring value by demonstrating new, relevant, impactful, or insightful knowledge even without top empirical scores; assess the overall contribution instead of SOTA alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation expectations and contemporaneous work
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors are encouraged to cite and compare with relevant recent work; 'contemporaneous' works are defined by publication timing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Papers published (in proceedings) within the last four months of the submission deadline are considered contemporaneous (and authors may be excused for not comparing to very recent non-peer-reviewed arXiv-only work). Reviewers should use judgment and consult their AC if unsure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflict of interest handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid reviewing papers with conflicts of interest and report conflicts when they arise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep OpenReview profile up to date to aid automated COI detection. If you find a conflicted paper during bidding, mark it 'Very Low'. If assigned a conflicted paper, contact the program chairs immediately to have it re-assigned.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to contact the area chair (procedural)
rubrics_metrics.description: Contacting the paper's AC should be done through OpenReview official comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While logged into OpenReview, add an official comment on the paper and add the AC(s) to the list of 'Readers' so they can see the message.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure and tone of the written review
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviews should be polite, precise, concrete, and constructive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize contributions positively and generously; list strengths and weaknesses comprehensively; be specific (include references when asserting prior work or novelty issues); provide actionable suggestions and clearly indicate uncertainties. Follow the principle of 'criticising with kindness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of good/bad reviewing practice (learning from exemplars)
rubrics_metrics.description: Concrete example reviews illustrate well-structured accept and reject reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good reviews provide a clear summary, enumerate pros and cons, request focused ablations or clarifications where needed, list typos/errors, and explain reasoning for the recommendation. Reject reviews should still provide constructive analysis and specific concerns that led to rejection (e.g., missing comparisons, lack of generality, insufficient analysis).
